name: Metric library
summary: Define each number goals are measured by once (its meaning and calculation, unit, direction, source and owner), and say which metric measures a goal, for a team or the whole company.

tables.name: okr_metrics
tables.purpose: The metric library: one row per metric, never deleted (removed_at when removed).

tables.name: okr_goal_metrics
tables.purpose: Which metric measures a goal, and for which slice (a team, or the whole company when team_id is null): one row per goal, removed_at when unlinked.

rebuild.builds: The metric library, and the worked example of a module with records of its own. A metric (name, meaning and calculation, unit, decimals, which way is better, source and its owner, refresh, owner, caveats) is defined once per workspace, and a goal links to one metric for a slice (a team, or the whole company), the goal’s own target being the target in it. Anyone adds a metric; its owner or an admin changes or removes it; the goal’s owner or an admin links and unlinks. Every change is logged, removing and unlinking keep the row and come back with Undo or Recently removed, and the AI tools do the same under the same rules. Its two records are its own, not the core’s: the module declares each (what one row is, its table, where a save and the workspace file it, whether it can be removed) with its rows each way, what a new cycle carries over (every metric not removed; the links in force to the cycle’s live goals) and how a removed metric comes back, and the core’s store, removal, restore, cycle and export keep them without knowing what they are. Its rules sit in its own folder, as pure as the core’s. Its own place, /metrics: the library (find by name, unit, owner or meaning; filter by unit, the team or the whole company a goal measures it for, owner, direction, unused, or something to sort out; sort A to Z, by most goals or by the latest change; 50 a page), a page per metric with its meaning, every goal measured by it side by side (status, slice, now, target, against plan) and what it still needs, an item in the menu after People, and the metric on a goal’s page and on a person’s and a team’s. “Measured by” in the goal forms: find a metric by typing (or add one there); choosing it on a new goal fills in its unit, decimals and direction; Goals filters by the metric. Defining one well: three things to be usable, the rest said later and named in words (“Fully defined” or “Still to say: …”, never a score), and three questions answered once before saving (a close name, a unit spelt another way, a percentage that doesn’t say out of what), with each Must fix and Check under its field. For, and which part: a link is for a team or the whole company and optionally one part of that number (“tier-1 services”), the parts in use offered under the field; the goal takes the metric’s unit and direction, its target stays its own; another goal on the same number, or a part spelt like one in use, is asked about once; and a goal with check-ins says why it is measured differently, in its History. Looking after one: what it still needs, a confirm before changing a unit or direction goals use, and on Workspace → About how many metrics have no owner.
entry: The core keeps a module’s own records (stage 2): a save carries them with the core’s, in one transaction; the workspace holds them by module and record; a removal saves them as changed, and Undo puts each back as it was just before.
Goals have a unit (metric and range goals) and teams have ids, so a link can check its unit and slice.
exit: A metric with a name, a unit and a direction saves; without any one of them it is refused with what is missing, and a second metric with the same name (any case) is refused.
Only a metric’s owner or an admin can change or remove it; only a goal’s owner or an admin can link or unlink the goal.
A goal in hours can’t be measured by a metric in minutes, and a goal with dated stages can’t be measured at all; a goal aiming the other way from the metric’s better direction links, with a warning.
A metric that has measured a goal can’t be deleted (“Retire it instead.”); one that never has is deleted, and Undo or Recently removed brings it back.

The demo workspace’s 13 metrics and 12 links load (two of them for one part: CI/CD · main branch pipelines, CI/CD · main pipelines), and every goal’s numbers, status and dates are exactly as without them (the conformance rows don’t move).
Built without the module, a workspace that holds its rows loads and saves, and none of its rows is changed or deleted; with the module back, they are all there.
Starting the next year carries every goal’s metric link to its copy: the same metric, team and part (journey U152; the core’s carry journey, U115, checks nothing of the module’s).

The library finds what each of rule 1’s worked examples says, a metric’s goals are rule 2’s rows in its order, and what a metric needs is rule 3’s, in order: every row of spec/conformance/metrics.csv matches.

The library is in the menu after People (under More on a phone); the old addresses of Metrics under Data lead to the library, a metric or the form; a metric’s row in the library counts the same goals by status as its page’s table lists (journey U81, checks F15 and N16).

In New goal, “Measured by” comes first on the measure step: a metric found by typing shows its meaning, fills in the unit, decimals and which way is better on a goal nobody typed them for, measures it for the goal’s team or the whole company, and Check says so; one added there is chosen; a goal with dated stages has none (journey U82, rule 5’s worked examples).

Adding a metric with a name close to one in use asks about it and still saves (rule 4’s worked examples); changing a unit or direction goals use asks first (the read-back, MT3); admins see on Workspace → About how many metrics have no owner (journey U83).

Adding a metric needs only a name, a unit and which way is better; its page then says what is still to say in words (“Fully defined”, or “Still to say: …”, and “Its owner has left.”), never a number, and every metric in the demo says the line rule 6 gives (the conformance rows `still`). A name a letter or a word from another’s or one a metric used to have, a unit spelt another way, and a percentage that doesn’t say out of what are each a Check answered once before saving, on the form and through save_metric’s checks and answers (rule 6’s worked examples; journey U105).

A link takes a part of at most 60 characters; a part spelt like one in use and another goal on the same metric, team and part are each a Check answered once; a goal with check-ins whose metric, team or part changes is refused without a reason, and the History entry gives it; the form offers the parts in use, and a goal’s About lists For, What it means, From the metric, where the number comes from and the goal’s own target (rule 7’s worked examples; journey U146).

Changing a metric goals use reads back first (MT3, rule 3): reworded caveats or a new name save at once; a new meaning or source asks “Is it still the same number?”, and “The number itself changes” is refused without a reason, then marks every goal’s chart (“Definition changed, week {w}”, a dashed hairline with its label beside it) and History, which Undo takes back; a new direction needs a reason and marks them too; a new unit is a new label (every goal’s unit changes in the same save) or a different scale, refused. Retiring a metric with goals keeps their links and numbers, leaves it out of the pickers and the library’s list, refuses a new goal it, and says so on each goal; Bring it back undoes that. Admins merge a metric into another in the same unit: every goal moves, the old one is retired pointing to the new, one Undo puts it back; a non-admin is refused (journey U106, rules 3 to 5’s worked examples).

A number source reads a metric for a link’s slice (a team or the whole company, and a part) or says it doesn’t, and passes the source contract; a reading’s state in a check-in is rule 1’s (no-slice, unreachable, missing, old after 7 days, same, jump, changed, fresh), and what a check-in records of it is rule 2’s, which nothing that judges a goal reads (the reading rule’s worked examples; the `reading` rows of spec/conformance/metrics.csv).

The check-in’s number step (the core’s place checkin.number) opens with a fresh reading in the field, “From {source}, read {when}.” and “Confirm {value} {unit}”; a different number asks why from four reasons before “Use {typed} {unit}”; a reading more than 7 days old is neither filled in nor shown; a company-wide source never fills in a team’s goal; the read-back says where the number came from; the one table fills fresh readings in the quiet ink and asks why in a changed row; and rule 3 (a differing number needs a reason) holds at the form, the table and post_check_in’s reading_confirmed and different_because alike (journeys U156 to U160). With the module off the step is as it was.
gaps: Owner-only rights and other governance, versions and draft states are left out on purpose (growth.md).
The goals table is where slices side by side and numbers read from the source would grow (growth.md: dimensions an admin defines; numbers from the source).
Left out on purpose and written down as ways to grow: spec/modules/metrics/growth.md.

growth.why: A metric is usable as soon as it has a name, a unit and a direction, which is all a team needs to start. A review step before anyone can use one would slow the first weeks for little gain at Faro’s size.
growth.how: Add a state to the metric (draft, ready), let goals link only to ready ones, and give whoever reviews definitions (a data owner, say) a list of drafts to approve. The rules page’s “who may” paragraph is where the new rule goes.

growth.idea: Versions, with a reason for each change
growth.why: Every change is already in the change log, field by field, with who and when, which answers “what did this mean in March?” for now.
growth.how: Keep each saved definition as a version with a required reason (as a goal’s plan keeps its earlier plans), show which version a goal’s numbers were read under, and let a reader compare two.

growth.why: Owners and admins can change a metric, as with goals. Stricter rules (only the owner, or changes approved by a data steward) need roles Faro doesn’t have.
growth.how: Add a steward role per metric or per source, and route changes through an ask to them (the asks model already carries who must respond).

growth.idea: Dimensions an admin defines, and slices side by side
growth.why: A slice is a team or the whole company, which covers how Faro’s goals are set. Other cuts (region, product, tier) and comparing slices need data Faro doesn’t hold.
growth.how: Let an admin define dimensions and their values, let a link name any of them, and add a view that lists every goal on one metric by slice, with their targets side by side.

growth.idea: Suggestions and grouping look-alikes for existing goals
growth.why: Linking is by hand, by each goal’s owner. Suggesting a metric for a goal, or spotting goals that measure the same thing under different names, needs matching that is easy to get wrong in a demo.
growth.how: Compare each unlinked goal’s title, unit and source with the library and suggest the closest metric; group goals whose definitions look alike and offer to link them all to one metric.

growth.why: A goal doesn’t have to be measured by a metric. Requiring one before a goal can be saved would block every workspace that hasn’t built its library yet.
growth.how: A workspace setting that makes every number goal need a metric, a flag (like the other attention flags) on goals that have none, and a count on Home for admins.

growth.idea: Loading the Metrics sheet back, and numbers from the source
growth.why: The Metrics sheet is written for reading, like Asks and Notes; metrics are added in the app or by an AI assistant. A goal’s numbers still come from its check-ins.
growth.how: Give the Metrics sheet match and edit columns and read it through the change engine (stage 2), as People is. Later, read each metric’s number from its source on its refresh cadence and offer it in the check-in.
